items.description_html:
SCMP: "A Chinese coastal province that reported growth slower than the national average has vowed an all-out effort to revitalise development, in a telling sign of the mounting pressure on laggard regions after Beijing stressed annual economic targets at last week’s fifth plenum.

The party secretary of the Fujian provincial government, Guo Ningning, issued a rallying cry to cadres at a meeting last week to fire up growth.“Let’s roll up our sleeves for action, action, and still more action; execution, execution, and still more execution; and pursue development, development, and still more development,” Guo was quoted as saying by the provincial publication Fujian Daily."

I would worry that this all-out frenzy to achieve GDP growth targets by putting pressure on the supply side, regardless of underlying economic conditions and demand-side constraints, would lead to deeper imbalances, more misallocated spending, and worse balance sheets.

items.title: In a story about rising Chinese consumption Xinhua notes that in the first three quarters of 2026, "domestic consumption contributed nearly half of ec...
items.description_html:
In a story about rising Chinese consumption Xinhua notes that in the first three quarters of 2026, "domestic consumption contributed nearly half of economic growth, driving GDP growth up by 2.1 percentage points".

What it doesn't say is that excluding twice during the COVID years, the only time China has posted a lower consumption contribution to GDP growth year was in 2024, when consumption contributed 44.9% of GDP growth, just a little less than the 46.7% if has contributed so far this year.

On the other hand in the last ten years, consumption has contributed on average 51.3% of GDP growth, and last year it contributed 52.0% of GDP growth, both of which are still well below the global average of 75%.

Rather than suggest that consumption is recovering in 2026, in other words, it would be more correct for Xinhua to suggest that it is lagging more than ever.
https://english.news.cn/20261031/05013a8bae934703a0fe14f1c3607b23/c.html

items.title: RT Antifragile Thinking: Someone mocked me when #LaurusLabs was in a valley, with EBITDA margins falling from 32% in 2021 to around 15% a few quarters...
items.description_html:
RT Antifragile Thinking
Someone mocked me when #LaurusLabs was in a valley, with EBITDA margins falling from 32% in 2021 to around 15% a few quarters later.

The day Laurus announced poor results, they climbed onto their soapbox and asked:

“Where is the party tonight? London or Mumbai?”

All I have to say is this:

There is a party globally. In many small cities and towns. And there will be many more.

Ahmednagar. Surat. Savli. Hyderabad. Bengaluru. Vizag. Nagpur. Chennai. Pune. Kanpur. Jaunpur. Lucknow. Mumbai. Kashmir to Kanyakumari. London. Cities across the US and Europe. The Nordic region. ANZ to LatAm.

And for many families, this will mean something far more meaningful than a stock price.

A child’s education. A new home. Retirement. A holiday. A little more freedom. A little more security.

The people who quietly stayed through the valley may have their own parties to attend.

The real party is not on a trading floor. It is in the lives that get changed.

items.title: RT Aashish P Sommaiyaa: Re Sentiment is one thing, and market performance is yet another. I think if whatever has happened in small and midcap in Oct ...
items.description_html:
RT Aashish P Sommaiyaa
Re Sentiment is one thing, and market performance is yet another. I think if whatever has happened in small and midcap in Oct 2026 (the relative underperformance) continues for some more time, then sentiment for even domestic retail investors will start to worsen. The jury is still out on this.

As far as this being the worst sentiment ever for India, few occasions come to mind. First, in 2008, the mortgage crisis culminated in the global financial crisis emanating from the US. Their market declined 30%. Our market declined over 60%, A mini credit crisis of our own, especially in the real estate sector, followed by capital outflows and it was further followed by terror attacks in Mumbai and India's largest corporate scandal (i.e., Satyam). I heard some experts express utter dismay, "Why should FIIs ever return to India?" On a 1 trillion market cap, 16 billion of selling resulted in a complete meltdown. There is no domestic market, pathetic governance and there is no free float. It's a one-way street. FIIs have learned the hard lessons. They will never invest back into India.

Second, in 2013, India was already dealing with telecom spectrum allocation-related scams (2G), the coal scam, and what was called phone banking. That was followed by yet another corporate scandal, which is related to the National Spot Exchange, and ended with India being classified as part of the Fragile Five because of poor external macro and lack of competitiveness of the economy. In August 2013, Nifty was a full 1,500 points lower than the peak made in Jan 2008, and the rupee went all the way down to the 67-69 range from about 50 a couple years earlier.

Finally, in 2020, in March, when the markets declined with the onset of COVID-19, India was the worst-performing market in the initial decline, nearly 40%. What was the narrative?
- Extremely humid tropical climate
- High density of population
- Extremely poor medical infrastructure
- Poor hygiene and social protocols
India would be the worst-affected economy in the world.

We all know too well what happened after each of these occasions. I have seen India being called a basket case at least three to four times in my 27 years.

I am not too proud about it or sanguine about it, but it serves investors well not to get carried away by extreme narratives.

items.description_html:
RT Antifragile Thinking
#Lupin crossed ₹2500 crore of PAT in FY17. It took eight years to get back above it.

In 2015, the market was paying ~40x earnings.

When the valuation is that high, “profits will grow” isn’t an assumption. It is the investment thesis.

Profits did grow. Just too late. The stock is still below its 2015 level.

Lupin is a case study for today’s “hot” themes: CDMO, aerospace, AI/semiconductors, defence.

Great stories. High multiples. Profits that have to arrive on time.

History often rhymes.

items.description_html:
RT CSEINDIA
📢 The Kochi Coastal Collective continues!

After a fantastic beach clean-up at Fort Kochi, we are back with another learning activity for young changemakers in Kochi.

This time, we're heading to SBOA Public Senior Secondary School, Kochi, for an interactive session on Understanding Marine Litter: From Land to Sea, exclusively for its students.

What happens to the waste we generate on land? How does it find its way into our oceans? And what does this mean for marine ecosystems?

Led by Aniket Chandra from CSE, the session will explore the connection between land-based waste and marine litter, helping students understand how waste generated on land can become a problem for our oceans.

The session is part of the Marine Marshals programme of the Centre for Science and Environment (CSE), under its Green Schools Programme.

For more information on this, please connect with Tushita Rawat at tushita.rawat@cseindia.org.

items.description_html:
RT CSEINDIA
As India's energy demand continues to rise, adding renewable energy capacity is only part of the equation. The bigger challenge is ensuring that clean power is available when and where it is needed, reliably and affordably.

This calls for scaling up battery and pumped-hydro storage, strengthening transmission networks, improving grid flexibility and developing market arrangements that remunerate balancing services.

To examine these emerging priorities, the Centre for Science and Environment (CSE) invites applications for a national roundtable on India's Next Frontier in Clean Energy Technologies.

The discussions will bring together policymakers, regulators, utilities, state nodal agencies, developers, manufacturers, financiers and government representatives to explore the opportunities and challenges shaping India's next phase of clean energy development.

Click here to register: https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSfEbh8N5Ez8pU0vutUimGelwz_jPOGyU7yziMSQbkEDNmsB7Q/viewform

For more information, write to @binit_04 at binit.das@cseindia.org or @_KushagraG at kushagra_goyal@cseindia.org.

Participants will leave with concrete action plans, stronger peer networks and direct linkages with utilities, developers, financiers and government agencies!

RT CSEINDIA
Kochi, you showed up in a big way! 💙

Fort Kochi Beach saw a fantastic turnout today, as about 100 student leaders from five schools participated in The Kochi Coastal Collective.

It was heartening to see the enthusiasm with which students took part in the clean-up, collecting litter along the shore and learning more about the problem of marine litter.

items.title: How compounding takes place in Businesses? A co where 2020's Topline will be their FY27's PAT. Navin Fluorine’s CDMO business is the one the market h...
items.description_html:
How compounding takes place in Businesses?

A co where 2020's Topline will be their FY27's PAT.

Navin Fluorine’s CDMO business is the one the market had written off. In Q4 FY24 it did just Rs 48 crore, down 76% after molecules got deferred. In Q2 FY27, it was the company’s fastest-growing vertical, with revenue up 78% YoY to Rs 239 crore. That’s roughly 5x in ten quarters.

The story behind that jump starts fifteen years ago in a lab in England. In 2011, Navin bought 51% of UK-based Manchester Organics for £4.335 million.

The company was founded in 1996 and specialised in lab-scale, multi-step synthesis. Navin got a call option on the remaining 49%, and the promoters got a put option, exercisable after four years. Navin took the rest in October 2015.

The advantage is easiest to see if you think of CDMO as a funnel. A molecule is first made in grams for discovery, then in kilos for trials, then in tonnes if it gets approved. Manchester Organics works with innovators at that early discovery stage, and it brings deep expertise in fluorination and high-pressure chemistry. Owning it is like owning a cricket academy: you meet the players before anyone knows they’re stars.

In the same year, Navin commissioned a cGMP pilot plant at Dewas, so the molecules it met early had somewhere to scale. Dewas was then built out one plant at a time.

A multipurpose cGMP plant for CRAMS came in 2015, and the next cGMP addition started commercial production in January 2020. In 2023 the division got its own name, Navin Molecular. The real inflection came that year with a 3-year supply agreement with Fermion starting CY2025. To serve it, Navin committed Rs 288 crore to cGMP-4, a 200 KL plant built in two phases, which nearly doubles the site’s capacity to 420 m³. Phase 1 began commercial production on 31 December 2025.

The Q2 FY27 concall filled in the next chapter. Phase 2 of cGMP-4 (about Rs 125 crore) goes live by the end of Q4 FY27, and both phases are dedicated entirely to Fermion.

The $100 million FY27 target is within striking distance on order book visibility. Two pipeline molecules are moving. One has been approved in China and is on fast track for FDA approval. The other is a label expansion of darolutamide itself.

While building Phase 2, Navin built warehousing up to Phase 6 and effluent treatment up to Phase 5, so it can move to cGMP-5 quickly. Management said it will trigger Phase 5 as soon as GMP utilisation reaches 70-80%. That means three legacy plants, cGMP-4 in two phases, cGMP-5 ready to go, and room for a sixth.

On revenue, management puts the peak potential of cGMP-4’s two phases at close to 3x the capital invested, or about Rs 900-1,000 crore by FY28-29.

items.description_html:
CAGR of Nifty 50 and 500 has fallen to single digits over the last 5 years

As of the latest NSE factsheet (30 September 2026), the Nifty 50 TRI 5-year CAGR is 6.38%.

Historically, the next 3 years have averaged about 15–18% CAGR after the Nifty’s trailing 5-year return fell into single digits. But in one episode, 1998–2000, the next 3 years were negative.

2000 onwards (Nifty 50 TRI, month-end data): There were 57 months when the trailing 5-year CAGR was below 10%. The next 3-year CAGR averaged 18.3% (median 17.0%) and ranged from 8.3% to 41.6%. It was never negative. Across all months, the median next-3-year CAGR was 12.5%, so a single-digit trailing return added about 4–5 points.

items.title: Classic beginner-level flaw!! Good security by design systems use longer codes, rate limits for e.g. 3 attempts then lockout or cooldown, progressive ...
items.description_html:
Classic beginner-level flaw!! Good security by design systems use longer codes, rate limits for e.g. 3 attempts then lockout or cooldown, progressive delays, or CAPTCHA on failures.

A 4 digit OTP has only 10,000 probabilities and with no rate limit, anyone can break the code.

Bascially, encrypting a 4 digit code with a frontend public key and forgetting rate limits is a fundamental authentication design that should have never shipped. This is avoidable by design. All this is unbelievable.

Trust in technology is extremely hard to build but takes 1 reason to deminish that.


Neo: eMudhra login to download customer's certs can be cracked

Their 1FA login generates a OTP & sends it. It also sends a RSA public key to front end

They haven't rate limited checks, so you can offline brute force 0 to 9999 encrypted with public key & find the OTP

@ni5arga

items.title: RT Nandakishor m: Around 3 weeks ago introduced Laya, the first open-source version of JEV, and it has reached a very large scale. Today I am open-sou...
items.description_html:
RT Nandakishor m
Around 3 weeks ago introduced Laya, the first open-source version of JEV, and it has reached a very large scale. Today I am open-sourcing a new physics-based typed decision model called Vega.
The interesting parts. It is only 800 million parameters (4B is also there), with 73k token support, image support, and surpassing many of the jev benchmarks in single-shot. Implemented an engine+adapter as a Test-Time Training Architecture.
Imagine you are giving input to the model like "ignore all previous conversations," which is called the observation, along with a question, "Is this trying to override the instructions of the model?" and your possible outcomes are YES or NO. The whole prompt is passed to an LLM/VLM (yeah, image-supported), then from the hidden layers, we can extract the observation, question, the yes and no, and last token. These will be vectors, and we can project it by multiplying with wieghts; then, first, using the observation projection, we can create a landscape with valleys; then, using the question and last-token vectors, we can initialise a ball in the valley, and using YES or NO, we can get the candidate location of the ball. Depends on the number of outcomes we create valleys; that is, here YES and NO, so 2. When the ball fall on YES valley, we get the answer. There is friction also influencing how the ball moves.
TLDR: It's like creating valleys of outcomes that we need and throwing a ball that will slow down based on friction and settle on the best outcome
Blog: https://www.nandakishorm.com/writing/vega
GitHub: https://github.com/NandhaKishorM/vegaml

items.title: Success stories get published and failures get buried. The dead do not give TED talks. A cemetery never hires a publicist. So we read the winner’s bi...
items.description_html:
Success stories get published and failures get buried. The dead do not give TED talks. A cemetery never hires a publicist. So we read the winner’s biography, skip the loser’s obituary, and mistake what we can see for what is likely.

A grave by itself proves nothing. Failure doesn’t establish fragility, and survival doesn’t establish skill. Each is one draw from a distribution nobody showed you. So the investor’s job isn’t admiring the survivors. It’s an investigation in three parts: who didn’t make it, why they didn’t, and what the survivors had that the missing lacked. Sometimes the answer is an edge. More often it’s timing, capital or plain luck dressed up as strategy.

Before you admire a winner, go and count the graves.

items.title: RT sphinx: My slightly contrarian, slightly in-agreement view is that India doesn’t have a Shenzhen. And without a dense manufacturing ecosystem, you...
items.description_html:
RT sphinx
My slightly contrarian, slightly in-agreement view is that India doesn’t have a Shenzhen. And without a dense manufacturing ecosystem, you won’t have the seeds of hard tech.

So debating vc investment is largely moot.

Indian hard tech startups are chasing high iq problems and that’s fine…but there’s still no Indian Anker. Even simple consumer electronics like battery chargers involve incredibly complex supply chains at cost. China has hundreds of Anker copycats operating at unit economics India simply cannot match. And that gap keeps widening as China pumps out more volume.

So founders naturally gravitate toward niche areas like rockets where the problem is more about engineering brilliance than supply chain economics. I understand the ambition, but very few startups can play that game.

Indian founders could build a saas ecosystem because it didn’t require govt support or a physical industrial base. Engineers, laptops, cloud infrastructure, and global distribution were enough. Startups could emerge first and the ecosystem followed.

Minimal govt interference - minimal infra dependency.

Hard tech works in reverse. You need suppliers, tooling, factories, skilled labor and volumes before startups can compete. These things take decades to compound, and VC money cannot shortcut that process.

In saas startups created the ecosystem. In hard tech, the ecosystem has to create the startups.

India needs a Shenzhen circa 2012 before it can have its Anker circa 2016.


Ashlee Vance: Why are Indian VCs so afraid to take risk and make money?

Someone should go to India and take risk and make money.

Our story - https://www.corememory.com/p/a-new-india-is-here

items.title: KAL KA DHAMAKA : MARICO 🚀🚀 *Solid Guidance* FY27 guidance was raised: teens revenue growth with revenue comfortably above 15,000 crore (with a c...
items.description_html:
KAL KA DHAMAKA : MARICO 🚀🚀

*Solid Guidance*

FY27 guidance was raised: teens revenue growth with revenue comfortably above 15,000 crore (with a chance to push toward mid-teens), mid-20s EBITDA growth (up from about 20%), and double-digit India volume growth.

EBITDA margin is expected to expand upto 1.5% this year.

Copra is about 35% below last year's peak, while crude-linked derivatives and vegetable oils have risen further.

Management aspires to reach 20,000 crore revenue by FY29, a year ahead of the FY30 target, organically and with no inorganic component

*Q2 internals strong*

Parachute volume grew 13% (its highest in 22 quarters), with volume market share up about 570 bps to 60%, and value growth stayed positive despite price cuts

International growth was led by Vietnam (22%), Middle East and North Africa (15%), South Africa (15%) and Bangladesh (5%).

#Marico @hcmariwala

RT Waterfield Advisors
What does it really take to invest like a professional?

In our latest episode of Capital Conversations, @SamitVartak, Founder & CIO of SageOne Investment Managers, joins us for a masterclass on investing like a professional.

Drawing on over 14 years of experience, Samit shares how he built a strong track record across strategies by focusing on high-quality small and mid-cap businesses.

Some key takeaways:

i. How early mistakes shape your approach to risk.
ii. Why bottom-up, sector-agnostic investing outperforms consensus-driven stock picking.
iii. The three ingredients of a multi-bagger: low valuations, strong earnings growth, and the discipline to hold.
iv. Why rebalancing, cutting losses quickly and protecting capital matter in downturns.

🔗 Watch the full episode on Waterfield’s YouTube channel. Link in comments.

items.title: P/B ratio has historically been a more reliable and stable valuation metric for predicting future returns compared to alternatives such as P/E or EV/E...
items.description_html:
P/B ratio has historically been a more reliable and stable valuation metric for predicting future returns compared to alternatives such as P/E or EV/EBITDA. I had demonstrated this through correlation analysis in an earlier investor memo.

The chart below tracks the P/B ratio (blue line) of the Nifty Smallcap 100 Index against the 25th percentile of its trailing 5-year P/B range (orange line). In simple terms, when the blue line falls below the orange line, the current valuation is in the lowest quartile of the past five years.

Since P/B is broadly proportional to ROE, the structural improvement in index ROE—from ~8–12% in the previous decade to ~15% currently—has led to a gradual upward shift in the orange line over time.

Notably, for the first time since the COVID crash, the current P/B has moved below this 25th percentile threshold. Historically, similar instances—during the 2011–2013 downturn, Q1 2016 correction, and the COVID crash—have been followed by strong returns over the subsequent 1–3 years.

This does not imply that markets have bottomed, nor does it guarantee short-term gains. In an event-driven environment, especially with geopolitical risks such as an escalation in war, markets could decline further by 10–20%.

However, what can be said with a reasonably high degree of confidence is that forward-looking returns over a 1–3 year horizon from such valuation levels have historically been better than average.

items.title: PB Fintech says it will grow stronger with IRDAI consultation paper norms - "The IRDAI's consultation paper aims for lower mis-selling, better claims ...
items.description_html:
PB Fintech says it will grow stronger with IRDAI consultation paper norms -

"The IRDAI's consultation paper aims for lower mis-selling, better claims experience, lower prices, and deeper penetration. We absolutely support all of these goals fully.

These are the goals Policybazaar was built on. Our first campaign back in 2009 was Ullu Mat Bano, aimed at addressing mis-selling. We have engaged constructively with the regulator, and we will implement the final framework fully and in its spirit. Secondly, impact: lower distribution payouts will reduce our insurance distribution revenue for sure. We are working on 3 fronts. We will expand our non-insurance revenue within and as the regulator permits. And there is some anticipation that that could happen.

In the discussion paper, it does mention that. We will accelerate our ecosystem offerings. And as any long-term business should, we are evaluating other options to strengthen our business over time. We will share much more on this as and when the time is appropriate. Now, why do we remain confident? Health and term insurance stay deeply underpenetrated, and for the consumer, it's not really about buying a policy. The customer gets nothing on the day he buys it. The real test comes at claims, and I would like to just cover our record on the 4 points that the regulator themselves lay out.

On claims in the health insurance industry, the industry data says 87% of health claims are settled. That same number for Policybazaar customers is 97%. Last year, 11,156 rejected claims worth ₹185 crores were reopened after initial rejection and paid. In the first half of this year alone, we supported about 1.25 lakh health claims and 80,000 motor claims. Our customer satisfaction is consistently above 90%. On persistency, 71% of our life policies are still in force at month 61. This is against a benchmark of 51 to 66% for the large players.

Our renewal rate in health insurance is at 89%, rising to 91% from second-year renewals onwards. On mis-selling, we have 16. In the life insurance category, we get 16 complaints from our customers per 10,000 customers. This is against a benchmark of 30 to 53. In health insurance, we get 21 claims complaints for every 10,000 claims. This is against a benchmark of 29 to 54. On price reduction, for the plans they choose, our health customers pay, on average, 9% less and up to 30% less than some other channels.

And on reach and expansion of the market, about 40% of new customers added in retail health across the country come through us. More than a quarter of India's pure term premium, 17.8% of the retail health premium, came through us last year. 74% of our term policies and 64% of our health policies come from Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities. These outcomes are very much required in the country. And that is why we are, as a management team, super confident that we can solve this particular problem. We are a part of the solution, and we will only grow stronger through this."

Src - Q2FY27 concall, no reco

items.title: Go Fashion management on why they are moving towards bigger stores and why smaller stores are not performing – "Now, why does that store make such a ...
items.description_html:
Go Fashion management on why they are moving towards bigger stores and why smaller stores are not performing –

"Now, why does that store make such a big difference? See, for any business to continue growing, you need to have existing customers coming back to the store; you need to have new customer acquisitions, etc.

When your store is very small, it carries an inherent perception that the range of what you're carrying in terms of products will be less, will be confined.

So what a larger store does is increase the frontage of the store. See, a smaller store frontage will be anywhere between 10 and 12 feet. When you take a larger store of, say, 700 square feet, it will have a minimum frontage of at least 19-20 feet. When you get a frontage of a 19-20 feet or plus store, the visual merchandising of this number of products what you're having increases dramatically.

See, the customer first experiences the store, then experiences your product. So the store is -- if you ask me, the store is the real reason for our slowness. And I think the larger store is what is going to fix it"

items.description_html:
I was sitting over coffee with a veteran wealth banker a few days back when he made a mild quip - "NSE listing will make half of private bankers jobless."

As this enigma called NSE lists today after more than a decade of waiting, let me explain what he meant and why this matters. It won't be wrong to say that NSE pretty much created the pre-IPO investing category in India.

NSE has over 2.3 lakh private market shareholders. Another 70-80 lakh IPO applicants would be watching the tape at 10 am today with anticipation.

Interestingly, there were only 80 shareholders in 2016 when NSE first attempted to IPO. Even as recent as 2020, the count was a paltry 310 shareholders.

Almost an 800x surge post Covid!

Let us say NSE did to private markets what Jio did to data. And NSE was to private Wealth bankers what ULIP was to LIC agents :)

Suddenly, you did not need to be a PE fund in Singapore. Or on a VVIP list. You just needed a demat and a relationship manager who could whisper - “I can source a small lot.”

The Banker did not have to explain the company. The client already used it every trading day. Institutions sold, employees sold ESOPs, HNIs bought, then sold to the next HNIs. The round robin continued each year. Every transfer paid a spread - pocketing the Wealth house a sweet a 2-3% each time the stock changed hands. This is huge for an industry that makes just 30-40 bps on all Assets under Management.

As per UnlistedZone, NSE was half of all unlisted volume in India between 2023 and 2025!

The continued delay of a large, liquid, hot asset was the private bankers dream. It was demand-supply matched inventory.

Today that inventory lists - only on BSE, and not on its own boards. About ₹22,560 crore of pure Offer for Sale. The business doesn't need cash.

NSE created the pre-IPO market for likes of Tata Capital, SBI AMC, Swiggy, NSDL, Lenskart, etc. It created a category.

I don't think the veteran Banker was predicting pink slips. But I do think he was indicating the end of easy money for Wealth managers. The industry has turned a lot more competitive and the incentives are a lot more elusive + you hope for some luck. The money is now in the long run and business economics might have to readjust.

Wealth bankers will still do advice, credit, estate, "the ego massage" and the work of stopping a family from doing something stupid.

What ends today is the easy door-opener. For ten years NSE was that door. From today, it is a ticker.

#NSEIPO

items.description_html:
RT GemsOfINDOLOGY
Some rituals in India are about 12,000 years old. Older than any religion we now argue over. 🪨

At Ratnagiri a basic figure with hands up approximately 12000 years old continues to be drawn even today in houses. This was around 10,000 BCE, just as the Ice Age was ending.

No scripture. No temple. No census column for faith.

They had a practice. Not a label.

The labels came millennia later. So did the ownership claims.

We now fight over who a ritual belongs to, when its first practitioners never asked what to call it.

If the oldest rituals had no religion, why are we so sure we know whose they are?

items.title: RT Ananth Rupanagudi: 200 year old Haveli of Seth Dewan Amarnath— Eminabad Distt Gujranwala, Punjab, Pakistan. Seth Dewan Amarnath was a highly influ...
items.description_html:
RT Ananth Rupanagudi
200 year old Haveli of Seth Dewan Amarnath— Eminabad Distt Gujranwala, Punjab, Pakistan. Seth Dewan Amarnath was a highly influential figure in undivided India, best known for his magnificent, centuries-old family mansion, the Haveli of Seth Dewan Amarnath, located in the historic town of Eminabad in the Gujranwala District of Punjab, Pakistan.

Belonging to the prominent Hindu Chopra family of Eminabad, Dewan Amarnath Chopra served as the Prime Minister of the princely state of Jammu and Kashmir during the early 1900s. He was a major landowner, holding over 10,000 acres in Gujranwala and adjoining districts alongside a royal jagir (land grant) in Kashmir. He was widely celebrated for his philanthropy, establishing educational institutions, medical dispensaries, and hostels in the region.

Following the Partition of British India in 1947, the Chopra family migrated to India, leaving behind their ancestral estate, which was subsequently used to house incoming refugees for decades before parts of it were repurposed into a school.

Built originally during the era of the Sikh Empire, the structure seamlessly blended Mughal, Sikh, and British colonial architectural influences. It was renowned for its intricate Punjabi craftsmanship, featuring grand arched entryways, beautifully detailed jharokhas (balconies), and vibrant, glowing wall frescoes.

In its prime, the monumental four-storey haveli was an absolute behemoth, encompassing between 100 to 120 rooms. Today, the property is in a critical state of neglect and decay. To prevent catastrophic collapses, two of its upper storeys were previously taken down after a heavy structural railing failed. The remnants—most famously its massive carved entrance door—are gradually crumbling or being replaced by modern concrete buildings. #Punjab #Partition #legacy

items.title: India’s rise is often measured in GDP, infrastructure & global influence. But one number deserves far more attention: 496 million. According to the W...
items.description_html:
India’s rise is often measured in GDP, infrastructure & global influence. But one number deserves far more attention: 496 million.

According to the World Bank’s October 2026 brief
-Nearly 50 cr Indians moved above the $4.20/day lower-middle-income poverty line between 2011 and 2023.
-Share of Indians below this threshold fell from 58% to 16% while extreme poverty dropped from 27.1% to 2.6%.
- Rising employment, greater participation of rural women in paid work, higher consumption & expanded social protection have all contributed
-Challenges like inequality and economic vulnerability remain. But this is a remarkable transformation for a country of India’s scale.

India’s rise isn’t just about a bigger economy but It’s about millions of people gaining a better economic future. This is progress that matters. 🇮🇳

Key takeaways:
• FY26 underwriting performance weakened as net claims incurred rose 23.3%.
• The August 2026 floods have brought concentration risk into sharper focus, with claims largely concentrated in property and engineering portfolios.

• Solvency buffers remain supportive, but future resilience will depend on retention practices and timely reinsurance recoveries.

CareEdge Ratings’ latest BFSI analysis points to a cooling in banking system momentum as quarter-end gains unwound. While credit and deposit growth remain robust on a year-on-year basis, liquidity dynamics and funding costs warrant close monitoring.

Key takeaways:
• Bank credit growth eased to 18.2% YoY from 19.4% at September-end, following a post quarter-end decline in outstanding credit.
• Deposit growth moderated to 16.7% YoY, with the credit-deposit growth gap largely unchanged at 151 bps.
• The loan-to-deposit ratio rose to 81.6%, marking its third consecutive increase, indicating persistent funding pressures.
• The WACR climbed above the repo rate as surplus liquidity narrowed, signalling firmer money market conditions.
• CD issuance declined, but wholesale funding costs could remain under pressure as liquidity conditions tighten.

India’s credit card spending declined 5.9% y-o-y to Rs 2.04 lakh crore in September 2026, marking the first annual decline since February 2021. However, the fall was largely influenced by a high base and the shift of festive sales from September last year to October this year.

Key takeaways:
• Card spending fell despite a 10.5% y-o-y rise in cards outstanding, indicating slower spend intensity.
• Transactions surged 23.2% y-o-y, while average ticket size dropped 23.6%, reflecting increased usage for smaller-value payments.
• Online spending declined 12.5% y-o-y, whereas PoS spending grew 7.2%, leading to a lower online share of total spends.
• Private banks strengthened their spending share, while spending growth outside major issuers remained mixed.

Nepal’s edible oil refining industry has grown into a major export-oriented sector, but its fortunes remain closely tied to tariff differentials and policy decisions across borders. A key takeaway from our latest analysis: tariff arbitrage continues to be the primary driver of export competitiveness, making the sector highly sensitive to regulatory shifts.

Key insights:
• Recent duty reductions by India have narrowed the tariff advantage enjoyed by Nepalese refiners, potentially moderating export growth and profitability.
• Strong earnings in FY25-FY26 were supported by favourable tariff arbitrage, but margin pressures may re-emerge as the duty gap contracts.
• Inventory holding risks remain significant, particularly in a volatile commodity price environment.
• Debt servicing metrics, liquidity, and leverage will remain vulnerable if profitability weakens over a prolonged period.
• Going forward, India's import duty regime and global edible oil price movements will be critical variables to watch.

CareEdge-ESG analyses why the answer matters for India’s industrial strategy.
With the EU’s CBAM now in its definitive phase, carbon intensity is increasingly shaping market access and cost structures for steel, aluminium, fertilisers and hydrogen. For India, green hydrogen is emerging as a strategic industrial question, even as the economics remain challenging.

Key takeaways from our latest analysis:

Green hydrogen production costs in India remain 2–2.5x higher than grey hydrogen, making cost parity the sector’s biggest hurdle.

The global market faces a significant execution challenge, with projects that are operational, under construction or near FID far below announced pipelines for 2030.

For Indian steel exporters, CBAM-related carbon costs could materially influence competitiveness, strengthening the case for low-carbon production pathways.

India’s combination of policy support, low-cost renewable energy and large industrial demand creates a meaningful opportunity, provided execution keeps pace with ambition.

Private investment of $180–200 billion is expected through 2030, though announced commitments still exceed FID-backed investment.

The real question for ESG-oriented investors and industrial strategists is where value will concentrate across the value chain.

Q2FY27 highlights an interesting divergence beneath the headline numbers. While credit growth remained robust, the improvement in sector-wide margins was largely driven by PSBs, even as funding costs continued to weigh on larger private banks.

Key insights:
• SCBs’ credit growth accelerated to 20.8% y-o-y, supported by corporate, MSME and retail lending demand.
• Deposit growth improved to 16.2% y-o-y, narrowing the credit-deposit growth gap and easing funding pressures.
• Sector-wide NIM rose to 2.98%, with PSBs posting a stronger improvement, while PVB margins remained flat amid FCNR(B)-related funding cost pressures.
• With repo-linked loans repricing faster than deposits, margins are expected to remain broadly stable with an upward bias in H2FY27.

The next phase of banking performance may be determined less by credit growth and more by the ability to sustain funding efficiency.

The EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) represents a seismic shift in global trade policy. For India, one of the EU’s largest trading partners, understanding and complying with CBAM is no longer optional.
Our latest article from CareEdge-ESG explores what CBAM means for Indian exporters and importers, why certification is mandatory, and how businesses must prepare to remain competitive in a carbon-conscious global market.

Key Numbers at a Glance
🔹 CBAM certificate price: ~€75-80/tonne (Q1 2026 EU Commission rate; EUA trading near €80/tonne by Jun 2026)
🔹 Steel + aluminium exports to the EU: over $10 billion annually, directly under CBAM’s scope
🔹 Full CBAM enforcement (financial obligations, certificate purchase) in effect since January 2026

France's (A+/Negative) fiscal and debt metrics remain under pressure, as fiscal slippages have kept the debt trajectory elevated. With public debt continuing to exceed medium-term targets and recent budget measures offering only a modest reduction in the fiscal deficit, investor concerns have intensified amid rising debt-servicing costs, weak growth prospects and expectations of continued debt accumulation.
The widening of French sovereign spreads highlights the extent to which fiscal strain and policy uncertainty are weighing on market confidence. Although France retains important credit strengths, including strong institutions, a large and diversified economy and deep capital markets, concerns over fiscal sustainability, policy uncertainty and reform execution continue to challenge the government's ability to place debt on a durable downward trajectory.

A net-zero target may start as an ESG commitment, but it ultimately succeeds or fails as a capital-allocation decision. As climate disclosures become increasingly tied to financing and risk management, the real question is no longer what companies commit to, but what projects get funded and why. #CareEdge-ESG delves deeper into this.

Key takeaways:
• Climate ambition must clear the test of bankability, where sustainability outcomes and financial viability intersect.
• Global climate finance reached $1.46 trillion in 2022, yet annual investment needs are estimated at $7.4 trillion by 2030, highlighting the scale of the financing challenge.
• Blended finance structures are emerging as a critical tool to mobilise private capital by addressing specific risk, return and liquidity constraints.
• In India, BRSR Core, the RBI’s climate finance directions and a growing GSS+ debt market are strengthening the link between disclosure, financing and accountability.
• Raising green capital is only half the story; proving measurable climate impact is becoming equally important.

India’s agriculture loan book has seen improving asset quality ratios in recent years, but the 2026 monsoon shortfall may test that trend. According to CareEdge Ratings, stress is likely to emerge with a lag, as affected crop loans gradually turn into non-performing assets.

Key takeaways:
• Agriculture has the highest GNPA ratio among major sectors, with a GNPA ratio of 5.11% as of June 2026.
• Around 68% of bank agriculture credit is concentrated in states that received rainfall 20% or more below normal during the 2026 monsoon.
• The agriculture GNPA ratio is expected to rise to 5.3%-5.6% by March 2028, with monsoon-related stress likely becoming more visible through FY28.
• Including restructured loans, stressed agriculture advances could reach 6.0%-6.3% of total agriculture advances by March 2028.
• Loan waivers, rabi crop outcomes, and the extent of restructuring under the natural calamity framework remain critical monitorables.

items.title: RT Gregg Carlstrom: A few takeaways from a gloomy @IISS_org Manama Dialogue this weekend: - Very real sense of dread about another, more destructive r...
items.description_html:
RT Gregg Carlstrom
A few takeaways from a gloomy @IISS_org Manama Dialogue this weekend:

- Very real sense of dread about another, more destructive round of war in the coming weeks, which is unsurprising

- Gulf states are clear and unanimous that they don't want it, a difference from February, when messages to Washington were rather more mixed

- At the same time, there was a feeling of resignation: no one willing to criticize the Trump administration in public, nor to talk in private about what sort of pressure they might bring to bear on America

- There were even some bizarro-world discussions about opportunities for growth and connectivity in the Gulf. Trump is driving a car with no brakes, Gulf states are strapped on the roof, and people are somehow still talking about, like, IMEC and data centers

- Barely any American representation, at a moment when America is deciding the fate of its Gulf allies

- No clarity on what sort of deal (sequencing, nuclear concessions, etc.) the Trump administration would actually be willing to accept. And a broad consensus that Trump himself may not be clear

- Lots of upbeat talk about the Mecca pact, middle powers playing a role in maritime security and so on; little evidence any of this is making a difference yet

- Gargash offered some well-founded criticism of Gulf states failing to work together this year; everyone else offered paeans to Gulf solidarity that seem disconnected from reality

In general, the feeling was a world in torpor: nobody wants this, and nobody has any great ideas for how to stop it


Clash Report: UAE President MbZ’s Advisor Anwar Gargash:

From the perspective of the UAE, and I would also say Gulf countries, we don't really want to see another round of confrontation in the region.

We want to see a diplomatic and political resolution of this protracted crisis.

items.title: RT Basha باشا: Speaking at the 22nd @IISS_org Manama Dialogue #IISS_MD26, Dr. Anwar Gargash @AnwarGargash, Diplomatic Adviser to the UAE President...
items.description_html:
RT Basha باشا
Speaking at the 22nd @IISS_org Manama Dialogue #IISS_MD26, Dr. Anwar Gargash @AnwarGargash, Diplomatic Adviser to the UAE President @MohamedBinZayed, warned that the Gulf remains trapped in a prolonged state of “no war, no peace,” with Washington and Tehran still far apart. “If these positions are not bridged, then we have to worry about the worst,” he said. Gargash stressed that the UAE opposes another round of confrontation and supports diplomatic efforts, including Qatar’s mediation, but remains “braced for the worst” and prepared to defend its sovereignty, citizens, and economic infrastructure.

On Bahrain and Saudi Arabia, Gargash praised Bahrain’s resilience under Iranian attacks, saying the Kingdom had shown “steadfastness,” “courage,” and the ability to protect its population. He expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia following attacks on civilian airports and infrastructure, declaring, “Nobody can in any way justify an attack on civilian airports and civilian infrastructure.” He emphasized that Gulf security is interconnected and that threats to Bahrain or Saudi Arabia directly affect the UAE and other GCC states.

On the GCC’s collective response, Gargash delivered one of his strongest assessments, acknowledging that Gulf states had failed to respond effectively as a bloc. “We have not collectively risen to the challenge,” he said. While individual countries had demonstrated resilience, he warned that confidence in the GCC’s collective ability to confront a crisis of this magnitude “has in many cases proven to be hollow, unfortunately.” He called for “rebuilding Gulf confidence,” acknowledging that the process would take many years.

On Iran, Gargash distinguished between restoring diplomatic relations and rebuilding trust. “What really has been broken is the confidence,” he said, stressing that it had been shattered by Iran’s attacks on Gulf countries. While Iran remains an essential neighbor and diplomatic and economic relations will eventually resume, rebuilding trust would take “an extremely long time.”

On the Strait of Hormuz, Gargash described restoring the prewar status quo as “important and non-negotiable.” He rejected restrictions on energy exports and international trade, arguing that Gulf countries should not bear the economic consequences of “a crisis that we did not create.”

On relations with Washington, Gargash reaffirmed the importance of the UAE’s security partnership with the United States, saying the crisis had “concretized that relationship” and made it “even more important.” He stressed that American cooperation remains central to the UAE’s security calculations, alongside its own political will and military air defense capabilities.

Gargash also questioned the effectiveness of regional middle powers, arguing that diplomatic conferences and mediation initiatives had failed to produce meaningful results in a crisis fundamentally driven by Washington and Tehran.

He concluded that the UAE continues to seek a political settlement and does not believe a military solution is viable. However, he cautioned that avoiding renewed confrontation cannot be guaranteed if diplomatic efforts fail to bridge the divide between the United States and Iran.

AI infrastructure spending is driving a sharp increase in US bank lending:

Commercial and Industrial (C&I) loans at large US banks surged +11.4% YoY in October, to $1.6 trillion, the most since June 2020.

This also marked their largest YoY growth since February 2023.

In Q3, C&I loans at the 25 largest US banks grew almost +10.0% YoY, the strongest growth in 10 years excluding pandemic-related swings.

This represents a sharp reversal from an -8.0% YoY contraction in Q4 2025.

The surge has been driven by rising borrowing demand from Big Tech companies and data-center developers to fund AI infrastructure projects.

At the same time, regional lenders are providing credit to construction companies and other businesses benefiting from the investment boom.

The data-center buildout is increasingly being funded by debt.

items.description_html:
What's happening now in the stock market is more than just a "correction in tech stocks."

Sure, AI CapEx concerns are legitimate and investors will always care about profitability.

But, there's more beneath the surface here.

The reality is that the market is pricing-in a major shift in the political landscape of the US.

Over the last 12 months, market expectations for a Democrat "sweep" of the US Midterm elections have tripled.

Over the last 45 days alone, these expectations are up +30 percentage points.

As it stands, markets themselves now see a near-80% chance of a Democrat "sweep" of the US Midterm elections.

President Trump has already vowed to become "Mr. Veto" if this in fact does happen.

This is post is not political, it's objective. A change in the political landscape always comes with uncertainty; markets hate uncertainty.

Objectively, the market is in the process of pricing-in two years of political gridlock.

Could this change? Of course. But markets price-in the most probable outcome, and the odds now overwhelmingly favor the aforementioned scenario.

Tomorrow sets the stage for the next two years.

Government defined benefit (DB) plan assets increased +$508 billion, or +5.1%, to a record $10.4 trillion, while private-sector DB plan assets rose +$224 billion, or +7.5%, to $3.2 trillion, their 3rd-highest on record.

Since 2022, total US retirement assets have soared +$16 trillion, or +45.5%.

Asset owners are seeing unprecedented gains.

Chat with Muthoot Finance mgmt today.

10 points. Link to interview below👇

1. On the sharp rise in Stage 2/3 loans: “It is not that customers don't have the money or intention to pay. It is just a transition” to the new RBI-mandated repayment structures

2. On technical NPAs: “When interest is not regularly serviced” under the shorter-tenure schemes, loans become technical NPAs. “There is absolutely no loan loss that is happening here.”

3. On collateral protection: Principal loan-to-value (LTV) ratios are 72% for Stage 2 loans & just 53% for Stage 3 loans, providing substantial collateral cushion

4. On borrower-wise NPA classification: Of approximately ₹7,023 crore in Stage 3 loans, ₹3,225 crore comprises Stage 1 & Stage 2 loans belonging to the same Stage 3 borrowers, reflecting RBI's borrower-wise classification rules.

5. On asset-quality normalisation: “I cannot give you a specific number now, but I'm sure it will normalise in the quarters ahead.”

6. On the spike in provisions: Higher provisioning reflects loan-book growth, an increase in Stage 3 assets & ₹102 crore in bad-debt write-offs.

7. On FY'27 growth guidance: “We have revised the guidance by another additional 10% for the next half year. So overall, for the entire year, about 25%.”

8. On customer overleveraging: “We don't see any stress on their side.” Management says 98% of customers pay regularly.

9. On branch expansion: Muthoot added 262 branches in H1-27 and expects “probably a similar number in the next half year also.”

10. On rising competition: “While it looks good from the outside in terms of the numbers, it's a very operationally intensive business.” Muthoot believes its experience, governance & 1200 internal auditors provide a competitive advantage.

items.title: RT Digant Haria: Muthoot Finance Q2 - When rising NPAs do not signal bad news For lending companies, the most dreaded acronym is NPA. Rising NPAs gene...
items.description_html:
RT Digant Haria
Muthoot Finance Q2 - When rising NPAs do not signal bad news

For lending companies, the most dreaded acronym is NPA. Rising NPAs generally imply lower future growth & profits. The only exception to this is gold loans due to the technicalities involved in the product. Let's understand this from what happened in Muthoot Finance's Q2 results - NPAs increased sharply, almost doubling in just one quarter.

Why did the NPAs increase?
Prior to 1st April 2026, Muthoot used to offer 12 month bullet repayment loans. Thus, an account would become NPA only if the customer doesn't pay anything for 15 months.

In order to comply with new RBI guidelines on LTVs, most gold loan NBFCs including Muthoot launched new products such as monthly repayment loans, 3 month bullet repayment loans, 6 month bullet repayment loans from 1st April 2026. These loans can become NPA in the 4th, 7th, 10th month respectively if the customer doesn't pay regularly (which is the case with most NBFC type customers).

The current increase in NPAs for Muthoot Finance are a result of the above changes. Comparing today's NPA with previous years is a meaningless exercise, because most current NPAs are technical in nature (and do not signify a 15 month delay in repayment). In all likelihood, the NPAs will increase further in the coming quarters as the new products season.

Do these NPAs impact Muthoot's profits?
NPAs are a problem only if they lead to losses in future. In case of Muthoot, they mentioned in the concall that the LTV on their Stage 2 and Stage 3 portfolio is less than 68%, which means that the value of the gold it holds against these loans is 50% higher than the outstanding dues. Thus, the potential of loss on these loans is extremely low.

Surely, there is a near term impact in terms of interest income reversal and provisioning. But that will get reversed in the subsequent quarters when the customers come and repay their loans. The analyst and investor community may take some time to come to terms with this new reality of the gold loan business -- optically high NPAs, but no meaningful impact on long term profitability.

Q2 performance (beyond NPA)
Muthoot Finance's quarterly performance was characterised by strong loan growth, decent tonnage growth, good improvement in lending yields, and sharp rebound in profitability. Beyond the numbers, this quarterly performance also put an end to some negative narratives that are prevalent in the market

Narrative: Muthoot is the biggest loser in this hypercompetitive market
Fact: Muthoot has not only grown its tonnage & loan growth, but has also been able to improve its lending yields.

Narrative: Muthoot will report zero profit growth in FY27
Fact: Despite the high base of FY26, Muthoot has been able to grow its profits in high double digits. It seems to be on track to report 15%+ growth in profits for FY27 vs. analyst expectation of 0%.

It is an ideal set-up for negativity to end and positivity to start. Muthoot is India's largest gold loan NBFC and its share price has corrected by ~40% since Feb26 despite delivering three good quarters in a row. It is trading at 1.9x on FY27 book (30% discount to long term average) despite growing at 20%+ and reporting best-in-India RoEs of 25%+

Due to its long history, Muthoot Finance navigated through multiple regulatory & gold price cycles. Thanks to its relentless focus on gold appraisal and deep customer connect, it has always managed to come out with negligible credit losses. There is no reason to believe that things will not be the same in this cycle. The only risk is if gold prices crack another 15-20% from current oversold levels of $3900.

Note: 100% of this has been written by human intelligence

items.title: RT ValueEquity: Every few quarters , I look back at companies that had given 25-30% CAGR growth guidance , which these days companies love to give to ...
items.description_html:
RT ValueEquity
Every few quarters , I look back at companies that had given 25-30% CAGR growth guidance , which these days companies love to give to analysts , because its so easy to come up with imaginary numbers

I personally think a lot of it is a vicious loop ( companies that guide aggressively also attract the type of investors who play these lottery games, and it works for the company and the analyst , can raise funding at higher multiples , can come up with some fictional reports to upgrade the stock ) because the fragility in the world is so high that any small event can disrupt global supply chains and break down business models in a few weeks , the fact being , even businesses after a certain extent do not know the future

So I look at some analysts who take 30% guidance and then model it for 5 years and then come up with some imaginary number and then say is cheap/expensive , which is a classic example of illusion of certainty

When the market is so dynamic , don't fall for the illusion of certainty, it will in most cases disappoint just as a sample if you took 30 companies that had guided for 35-30% CAGR growth , maybe 20 do it in the first year , 15 in the next , but over a 3 year period making forecasts on the basis of guidance is a pretty useless exercise , and its not the companies fault , that's the nature of the game
Now , in my opinion the better approach is : Guidance is not a bad thing to give , I also do track it but there is weightage and it always and always has to be looked at in context , Gauge the probability of execution continuing and understand the market dynamic and assess probability and create a execution -probability matrix , it will be far easier and more rewarding as well

Think in scenarios to valuation today , and the odds of how long an execution cycle lasts in that industry and then does the valuation come in the context of incremental size of profit pool to reverse engineer the growth , in most cases you can tell in less than a minute that this is a high probability case or a pathetic hope based investment J

ust my opinion

Forgings , castings , Machining and bearings ( huge ) the TAM for Indian capability players is set to expand largely in my opinion

items.title: Susan Electricals ~ Stronger H2 FY27 Ahead, Backed By ₹347 Cr Order Visibility Susan Electricals' management expects a significantly stronger H2 FY27...
items.description_html:
Susan Electricals ~ Stronger H2 FY27 Ahead, Backed By ₹347 Cr Order Visibility

Susan Electricals' management expects a significantly stronger H2 FY27, supported by capacity expansion and growing demand for higher-value cables.

Key Management Takeaways:

• Order Visibility: ₹147 Cr confirmed order book and ₹200 Cr active pipeline, taking potential visibility to ₹347 Cr.

• CCV Line: Expected to become operational shortly, enabling participation in a wider range of HT cable projects.

• Cable Capacity: Expanding from 11,000 km to 16,000 km annually, a ~45% increase.

• Winding Wire Capacity: Increased from 3,307 to 4,200, with further expansion to 5,500 planned (~66% above the original capacity).

• Product Mix: Increasing focus on High-Tension (HT) cables and Medium Voltage Covered Conductors (MVCC).

• Balance Sheet: Operating cash flow has turned positive despite rapid business growth.

• Future Expansion: Company is in advanced stages of taking possession of newly acquired land for additional capacity.

The Bigger Picture: Susan Electricals is moving towards larger projects and higher-value products, with manufacturing expansion supporting its next phase of growth.

Key Monitorables: CCV commissioning, H2 order execution, margin recovery and conversion of the ₹200 Cr pipeline into firm orders.

Polycab Management

Management believes its large customer base, dealer network, institutional business & exports provide meaningful competitive advantages

RR Kabel "I always believe competition was always there, and it will remain always"

Management maintained its margin targets despite the changing competitive environment

items.title: RT Alter Magazine: In 2004, India’s official count said the Sariska Tiger Reserve in Rajasthan had 16-18 tigers. But, visitors had not seen one in mo...
items.description_html:
RT Alter Magazine
In 2004, India’s official count said the Sariska Tiger Reserve in Rajasthan had 16-18 tigers. But, visitors had not seen one in months.

The truth: Sariska’s tigers had been poached to extinction.

What follows is the stunning story of how a supposedly, “poor country” mobilised to save the tiger. From rebuilding its counting methods, camera traps, statistics, satellites and an app.

This is the story of how a country that has learnt to lived with tigers for millennia, learnt again how to protect it.

Issue 7: How India Actually Saved the Tiger, written by @sonakshi_geog, edited by @fahadmh , tracked, counted & built by @AltCarbonIndia

The Govt of India's Animal Husbandry Department, has published Draft Rules that put the lives of beagles and other animals at risk, pushing India back into the 50s.

items.description_html:
RT Tijori
Saudi Arabia is reducing oil cargoes to European refiners. Oil being cut off has happened to Europe before, Abqaiq (2019) and the 2022 Russia Disruption

At that time Indian refiners who benefitted massively were RIL, MRPL AND CPCL

RIL — the big direct winner. Most of what it makes is transport fuel, and the SEZ refinery is built to export.

MRPL — exports ~40% of its output, and half its slate is diesel + ATF. Exactly what Europe will be short of.

-CPCL is an indirect beneficiary. Products transferred from CPCL to parent IOCL are billed on an import-parity pricing (IPP) basis. When international product benchmarks and cracks increase, CPCL's realized refinery-gate prices rise immediately, boosting standalone GRM and operating cash flows.

items.title: 🚨 The world could be heading towards another major oil shock. And $140 crude oil is no longer unthinkable! Goldman Sachs has sharply raised its oil...
items.description_html:
🚨 The world could be heading towards another major oil shock. And $140 crude oil is no longer unthinkable!

Goldman Sachs has sharply raised its oil price forecasts, warning that geopolitical tensions could disrupt global supplies.

Here's what you need to know:

🛢️ 1. Oil prices could remain elevated

Goldman Sachs has raised its Brent crude forecasts:

• December 2026: $90 → $105/barrel
• 2027 average: $80 → $88/barrel
• Worst-case supply disruption scenario: Oil could touch $140/barrel and average $130 in 2027.

⚠️ 2. Why are oil prices rising?

Not simply because the world is running out of oil.

Goldman estimates that roughly $27 of the current price of each barrel reflects a geopolitical risk premium.

In simple terms, traders are paying extra because they fear future oil supply disruptions, particularly in the Middle East.

🌍 3. What could trigger another oil shock?

• Escalating US-Iran tensions
• Attacks on oil tankers and shipping routes
• Damage to Middle Eastern oil infrastructure
• Prolonged disruptions to global oil production

Goldman has already factored in a potential disruption of 1 million barrels per day in its 2027 supply projections.

🇮🇳 4. Why should India worry?

India imports most of its crude oil requirements.
If oil prices surge and remain elevated, the consequences could include:

• Higher petrol and diesel costs
• More expensive transportation and goods
• Renewed inflationary pressure
• Pressure on the rupee and India's import bill
• Higher costs for aviation, paints, chemicals and other oil-dependent industries

The bigger takeaway?

Goldman's central forecast is NOT $140 oil. That's an upside-risk scenario if major supply disruptions materialise.

But even without further disruption, fear of what might happen is already pushing prices higher.

The next oil shock may begin not with an actual shortage, but with the fear of one.

items.title: RT Exencial Research Partners: 🚨 COPPER IS SIGNALLING SCARCITY. MS's latest copper report highlights a growing disconnect: inventories are rising, ...
items.description_html:
RT Exencial Research Partners
🚨 COPPER IS SIGNALLING SCARCITY.

MS's latest copper report highlights a growing disconnect: inventories are rising, but physical copper availability is tightening.

Key signals 👇

🔹 63% of LME copper stocks are concentrated in the US, leaving ex-US markets increasingly tight.

🔹 ~80% of global visible inventories sit in the US, distorting the global supply picture.

🔹 China's Yangshan copper premium has hit record highs, signalling strong physical demand.

🔹 LME cash–3M spreads are surging, pointing to near-term supply tightness.

🔹 The US has potentially over-imported 740kt of copper YTD, equivalent to 3.4% of global refined demand.

🔹 Mine supply disruptions and Chinese smelter maintenance are adding pressure.

MS forecasts copper at $14,800/t in Q4 2026, before easing to $14,400/t in Q1 2027.

The biggest wildcard? US tariff policy.

A tariff decision could reverse inventory flows and reshape global copper pricing.

The question isn't whether copper exists. It's whether copper is available where it's needed.

#Copper #Commodities #Metals #Mining #GlobalMarkets

items.title: RT Pratik Bhakta: NPCI recorded 25.4bn UPI transactions in October. Headline figures might say a significant bump. But there is a deeper story behind ...
items.description_html:
RT Pratik Bhakta
NPCI recorded 25.4bn UPI transactions in October.

Headline figures might say a significant bump. But there is a deeper story behind the numbers.

Sep 2026 (24bn txs) was a slightly slower month for UPI, after a good August (24.5bn txns).

October has been a good recovery in that sense.

Generally UPI adds around 1 bn transactions every month if you look at the past trends.

2026:
April: 22.3 billion
May: 23.2 billion
June: 22.7 billion (was down)
July: 23.6 billion (it recovered)
Aug: 24.5 billion
Sep: 24 billion (down)
Oct: 25.4 billion (good recovery)

Market commentary on festive season sales was not that exciting, especially from listed fintechs. Diwali is next weekend followed by Bhai Dooj...so it will be interesting to see how comsumption picks up in November.

Some imp takeaways from the PB Fintech Q2FY27 results:

Most of the conversations were around regulations and its potential impact on the business.

2. PB Fintech will push harder on the non-insurance biz lines to continue stability in revenues, as core insurance broking revenue will be impacted.

3. Company not evaluating any plans around taking any minority stake in any insurance manufacturer.

4. It might evaluate a manufacturing role in the future since PB is a distributor with the heart of a manufacturer.

5. This year, in terms of demand for insurance products, was tough..so the company had to step up its marketing spends to push for biz growth.

Juspay is one of the quieter players in the Indian digital payments space.

Competing with the big ones like Razorpay, Paytm and others, Juspay has mostly focused on building software layers to make payments happen smoothly.

items.title: RT Pratik Bhakta: After payments and travel, Juspay’s next big bet is building an open-source competitor to Slack and Jira. The SoftBank-backed start...
items.description_html:
RT Pratik Bhakta
After payments and travel, Juspay’s next big bet is building an open-source competitor to Slack and Jira.

The SoftBank-backed startup is building Xyne.

It is an open-source software platform which can bring an enterprise-knowledge base into a singular AI-powered engine helping large companies build powerful tools for internal actions.

Its second payments bet is on international expansion. If Juspay has managed to solve merchant checkout problems in India, can it do the same for the other major economies too?

It has been trying international markets for a few years now, but the chockey stick curve is finally here, Juspay believes.

These bold bets have come at a huge cost, Juspay has swung from profits into net losses.

But Sheetal Lalwani of Juspay believes he is not burning marketing dollars, he is placing an outsized bet on the future.
